Normally, writes to the InnoDB buffer po: Normally, writes to the InnoDB buffer pool happen in the background. However, if it's necessary to read or create a page and no clean pages are available, it's necessary to wait for pages to be flushed first. This counter counts instances of these waits. If the buffer pool size was set properly, this value should be small.

The number of free memory blocks in quer: The number of free memory blocks in query cache. High numbers can indicate fragmentation issues, which may be solved by issuing a FLUSH QUERY CACHE statement.
The number of fsync() operations so far.
The number of fsync() writes done to the: The number of fsync() writes done to the log file.
The number of in-memory temporary tables: The number of in-memory temporary tables created automatically by the server while executing statements.
The number of internal COMMIT statements: The number of internal COMMIT statements.
The number of internal ROLLBACK statemen: The number of internal ROLLBACK statements.
The number of joins that did a full scan: The number of joins that did a full scan of the first table.
The number of joins that do not use inde: The number of joins that do not use indexes. If this value is not 0, you should carefully check the indexes of your tables.
The number of joins that used a range se: The number of joins that used a range search on a reference table.
The number of joins that used ranges on: The number of joins that used ranges on the first table. (It's normally not critical even if this is big.)
The number of joins without keys that ch: The number of joins without keys that check for key usage after each row. (If this is not 0, you should carefully check the indexes of your tables.)
The number of key blocks in the key cach: The number of key blocks in the key cache that have changed but haven't yet been flushed to disk. It used to be known as Not_flushed_key_blocks.
The number of latched pages in InnoDB bu: The number of latched pages in InnoDB buffer pool. These are pages currently being read or written or that can't be flushed or removed for some other reason.
The number of log write requests.
The number of logical read requests Inno: The number of logical read requests InnoDB has done.
The number of logical reads that InnoDB: The number of logical reads that InnoDB could not satisfy from buffer pool and had to do a single-page read.
The number of merge passes the sort algo: The number of merge passes the sort algorithm has had to do. If this value is large, you should consider increasing the value of the sort_buffer_size system variable.
The number of non-cached queries (not ca: The number of non-cached queries (not cachable, or not cached due to the query_cache_type setting).
The number of pages busy because they ha: The number of pages busy because they have been allocated for administrative overhead such as row locks or the adaptive hash index. This value can also be calculated as Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_total - Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_free - Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_data.
The number of pages containing data (dir: The number of pages containing data (dirty or clean).
The number of pages currently dirty.
The number of pages that have been writt: The number of pages that have been written for doublewrite operations.
The number of pending log file fsyncs.
The number of physical reads of a key bl: The number of physical reads of a key block from disk. If Key_reads is big, then your key_buffer_size value is probably too small. The cache miss rate can be calculated as Key_reads/Key_read_requests.
The number of physical writes of a key b: The number of physical writes of a key block to disk.
The number of physical writes to the log: The number of physical writes to the log file.
The number of queries added to the cache: The number of queries added to the cache.
The number of queries registered in the: The number of queries registered in the cache.
The number of queries that have been rem: The number of queries that have been removed from the cache to free up memory for caching new queries. This information can help you tune the query cache size. The query cache uses a least recently used (LRU) strategy to decide which queries to remove from the cache.
The number of queries that have taken mo: The number of queries that have taken more than long_query_time seconds.
The number of requests to insert a row i: The number of requests to insert a row in a table.
The number of requests to read a key blo: The number of requests to read a key block from the cache.
The number of requests to read a row bas: The number of requests to read a row based on a fixed position. This is high if you are doing a lot of queries that require sorting of the result. You probably have a lot of queries that require MySQL to scan whole tables or you have joins that don't use keys properly.
The number of requests to read a row based on a key. If this is high, it is a good indication that your queries and tables are properly indexed.
The number of requests to read the next: The number of requests to read the next row in key order. This is incremented if you are querying an index column with a range constraint or if you are doing an index scan.

The number of requests to read the next row in the data file. This is high if you are doing a lot of table scans. Generally this suggests that your tables are not properly indexed or that your queries are not written to take advantage of the indexes you have.
The number of requests to read the previ: The number of requests to read the previous row in key order. This read method is mainly used to optimize ORDER BY … DESC.
The number of requests to update a row i: The number of requests to update a row in a table.
The number of requests to write a key bl: The number of requests to write a key block to the cache.
The number of row locks currently being: The number of row locks currently being waited for.
The number of rows deleted from InnoDB t: The number of rows deleted from InnoDB tables.
The number of rows inserted in InnoDB ta: The number of rows inserted in InnoDB tables.
The number of rows read from InnoDB tabl: The number of rows read from InnoDB tables.
The number of rows updated in InnoDB tab: The number of rows updated in InnoDB tables.
The number of rows waiting to be written: The number of rows waiting to be written in INSERT DELAYED queues.
The number of rows written with INSERT D: The number of rows written with INSERT DELAYED for which some error occurred (probably duplicate key).
The number of sequential read-aheads Inn: The number of sequential read-aheads InnoDB initiated. This happens when InnoDB does a sequential full table scan.
The number of sorts that were done by sc: The number of sorts that were done by scanning the table.
The number of sorts that were done with: The number of sorts that were done with ranges.
The number of streams that are open (use: The number of streams that are open (used mainly for logging).
The number of tables that are open.
The number of tables that have been open: The number of tables that have been opened. If opened tables is big, your table_open_cache value is probably too small.
The number of temporary tables currently: The number of temporary tables currently open by the replica SQL thread.
The number of temporary tables on disk c: The number of temporary tables on disk created automatically by the server while executing statements. If Created_tmp_disk_tables is big, you may want to increase the tmp_table_size  value to cause temporary tables to be memory-based instead of disk-based.
The number of threads created to handle: The number of threads created to handle connections. If Threads_created is big, you may want to increase the thread_cache_size value. (Normally this doesn't give a notable performance improvement if you have a good thread implementation.)
The number of threads in the thread cach: The number of threads in the thread cache. The cache hit rate can be calculated as Threads_created/Connections. If this value is red you should raise your thread_cache_size.
The number of threads that are not sleep: The number of threads that are not sleeping.
The number of threads that have taken mo: The number of threads that have taken more than slow_launch_time seconds to create.
The number of times a row lock had to be: The number of times a row lock had to be waited for.
The number of times a row was deleted fr: The number of times a row was deleted from a table.
The number of times that a table lock co: The number of times that a table lock could not be acquired immediately and a wait was needed. If this is high, and you have performance problems, you should first optimize your queries, and then either split your table or tables or use replication.
The number of times that a table lock wa: The number of times that a table lock was acquired immediately.
The number of times the first entry was: The number of times the first entry was read from an index. If this is high, it suggests that the server is doing a lot of full index scans; for example, SELECT col1 FROM foo, assuming that col1 is indexed.
The number of transactions that used the: The number of transactions that used the temporary binary log cache but that exceeded the value of binlog_cache_size and used a temporary file to store statements from the transaction.
The number of transactions that used the temporary binary log cache.
The number of unused blocks in the key c: The number of unused blocks in the key cache. You can use this value to determine how much of the key cache is in use.
The number of used blocks in the key cac: The number of used blocks in the key cache. This value is a high-water mark that indicates the maximum number of blocks that have ever been in use at one time.
The number of waits we had because log b: The number of waits we had because log buffer was too small and we had to wait for it to be flushed before continuing.
The number writes done to the InnoDB buf: The number writes done to the InnoDB buffer pool.
